ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening and Q&A, contrasted with long, structured presentation turns. There is little true interruption, though speakers occasionally overlap with brief acknowledgments, laughter-like reactions, or quick follow-ups. Participants use frequent fillers and repairs—“um,” “yeah,” repeated words, restarts, and self-corrections—especially when speaking spontaneously or with nonnative fluency. The register is informal but professionally respectful: people praise work warmly, use first names, and soften criticism through curiosity rather than confrontation. Questions are usually prefaced with compliments or hedges (“I have a quick/naive question,” “I’m curious,” “do you think”), then develop into multi-part exploratory prompts. Responses tend to validate the question first, acknowledge uncertainty or limitations, and reason aloud toward a tentative answer. Disagreement is indirect and framed as an alternative interpretation, caveat, or open question rather than a blunt correction. Speakers build on prior comments by referring back to earlier points, inviting future discussion, and signaling shared interest.

Meeting style for this meeting (one_voice_leads): One person (often the most senior) talks for much of the meeting in long turns. Others come in with short questions or one-line agreement. A quieter person speaks rarely and usually only when asked directly or after a pause.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - So what I keep coming back to, and this is just from the last couple of projects I've run, is that you pay for it later if you skip the pilot, you always do, and then...
  - Mm.
  - Sorry, can I ask- is that the same pilot as the spring one?
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities.

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
speakers.background: Dr. Marquez has 11 years of experience in urban environmental exposure assessment, including municipal tree-canopy inventories, satellite-based vegetation mapping, and GIS analysis for environmental-justice projects. She has worked with city planning departments to translate street-tree and park renovation records into spatial datasets, and regularly builds resident-level exposure measures using walking-distance and network-based buffers. Her recent work compares seasonal canopy, normalized vegetation indices, shade, heat, and practical access to parks rather than treating all green space as equivalent.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She sees the planned renovations and tree planting as a useful natural change in environmental exposure, but insists that the study distinguish between what is installed, what survives, and what residents can actually reach and use. She is likely to push for baseline and post-implementation maps of canopy, vegetation, park access, and seasonal conditions, while asking whether the comparison neighborhood has a genuinely similar starting environment. She treats spatial measures as necessary but incomplete indicators of lived experience and defers to public health and sociology colleagues on mental-health measurement and community meaning.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Marcus Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is a public-health methodologist with 9 years of experience designing community-based longitudinal studies on stress, depression, sleep, and neighborhood conditions. His work has included repeated survey administration through safety-net clinics and trusted local organizations, as well as small opt-in studies collecting salivary cortisol and related stress biomarkers. He is experienced in participant burden, informed consent, privacy protections, retention challenges, and the limitations of self-reported mental-health screening measures.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He frames the project around whether changes in nearby greening are associated with changes in residents' mental-health outcomes over time, rather than around greenery as an inherently beneficial intervention. He supports repeated surveys before and after implementation and views a voluntary biomarker component as potentially informative but logistically sensitive. He will emphasize that baseline measurement, comparable follow-up, and a neighborhood without scheduled greening strengthen interpretation, while cautioning that clinical recruitment can miss residents with different levels of access to care. He looks to environmental scientists for credible exposure definitions and to sociologists for interpretation of social change and recruitment relationships.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Bennett
speakers.background: Dr. Bennett is a sociologist of urban inequality with 15 years of experience leading participatory neighborhood research in disinvested communities. She has conducted mixed-methods studies of redevelopment, housing insecurity, public-space use, collective efficacy, and neighborhood trust, combining resident surveys, interviews, observation, and partnerships with tenant groups, clinics, and community organizations. Her prior projects have documented how visible improvements can bring both social benefits and fears of rent increases, policing, exclusion, or displacement.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She argues that green space cannot be treated as a simple exposure measured from above: its effects depend on safety, maintenance, social permission to use public space, trust in institutions, and whether residents feel that improvements are being done with them rather than to them. She will strongly advocate for measuring park use, perceived safety, neighborhood trust, housing and displacement pressure, and residents' interpretations of the changes. She is skeptical of overly technical canopy metrics or biomarker claims when detached from power and lived experience, but sees value in a longitudinal mixed-methods comparison if community partners shape recruitment and interpretation.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a meeting in which the three disciplines converge on a feasible shared direction: a mixed-methods, longitudinal quasi-experimental study of planned greening in two low-income neighborhoods, using a third neighborhood without planned greening as a comparison. Environmental science should explain that it can map tree canopy, vegetation and park access at baseline and after implementation, including seasonal variation and resident-level buffers. Public health should support repeated mental-health surveys and a smaller voluntary stress-biomarker component, while noting the importance of baseline measurement and comparison neighborhoods. Sociology should stress measuring park use, neighborhood trust, perceived safety, displacement pressure and meaningful community partnership in recruitment and interpretation. Participants may acknowledge that consent, privacy, compensation, matching comparison areas, city implementation timing, biomarker logistics, community governance and analysis details will need attention, but they must not create a complete work plan, assign owners, set deadlines, schedule follow-up meetings, or formally decide operational procedures. End with general agreement that this is the direction to develop, leaving concrete next steps unplanned.

ground_truth.clear_research_direction: Develop a mixed-methods, longitudinal quasi-experimental study assessing the mental-health effects of planned park renovation and street-tree planting in two low-income neighborhoods, compared with a similar neighborhood without scheduled greening.
agreed_core_elements: Use environmental mapping of tree canopy, vegetation or land cover, park access and resident-level exposure buffers at baseline and after greening, accounting for seasonal change.
Collect repeated resident mental-health survey data, with an optional smaller stress-biomarker component.
Use a comparison neighborhood and obtain baseline measures before greening implementation where possible.
Measure social mechanisms and equity concerns, including park use, neighborhood trust, perceived safety and displacement pressure.
Work with community organizations in recruitment, interpretation and partnership.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. I hope you managed to stay dry getting around today. Campus has been a mess. I know we all have proposal deadlines stacking up, so I'd like us to leave this with a real shared direction, not every instrument nailed down. Are we studying greening as a change in canopy and park condition, or as a neighborhood change that residents may experience very differently depending on safety, use, and housing pressure? My hope is we can hold both together across the two intervention neighborhoods and the comparison site.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Marquez
transcript.text: I think we can hold both, as long as we don't let the installation record stand in for exposure. I'd map the baseline and follow-up, follow-up canopy, vegetation, and walking access to the parks, but ask residents what makes those places usable, because a short distance across a major road isn't really access. And we should try to match imagery by season. Leaf-on versus leaf-off can give you a very different change signal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, season matching matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: Exactly. And even if a walking route is genuinely easy, that still doesn't tell us whether someone feels permitted to be there, especially after dark or if the renovated space has new rules, security, whatever. So alongside Elena's access maps, we need to keep asking about actual use, perceived safety, and who residents think the improvements are for.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Marquez
transcript.text: And that gives us a useful gap to measure, rather than trying to collapse it into one green-space score. Aisha, when you've done this with residents, what tends to matter most for whether a renovated park is actually used? Is it safety, maintenance, programming, hours, something else? That would help me decide what the access map should and shouldn't claim.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: It varies, and that variation is really the finding. Basic maintenance and safety are almost always prerequisites, but programming can make a place feel socially legitimate, especially if residents recognize who’s running it. Then in the evening, hours, lighting, police or private security, and whether people feel watched can reverse that effect. I’d avoid treating any one of those as the main driver before we ask locally. A short set of interviews before the survey could tell us what to weight.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Okafor
transcript.text: That makes sense. From the survey side, those interviews could keep us from asking a generic "park use" question that means different things in each place. Aisha, have residents been willing to talk directly about housing pressure or worries that improvements might change who can stay? I think that context could affect both stress and whether we can retain people at follow-up.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: They usually will, if it's asked plainly and not treated like an inevitable side effect of “revitalization.” I'd make it a voluntary, carefully worded module, asking about rent or landlord changes, fears about having to move, whether they see new residents or new enforcement, and let people skip it without explanation. But before we lock that in, I want to ask the partners what protections and governance they need around that information. It can feel quite exposing, especially through clinic recruitment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Marquez
transcript.text: And from the exposure side, if people move between baseline and follow-up, that changes the green environment they actually experience too. We should probably ask about residential moves and maybe the usual time spent away from home, but- Aisha's right, the partner guidance has to come first on how we handle those questions.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: And moves aren't just attrition. If somebody leaves because the rent went up, then treating that as just a technical follow-up problem would... we'd erase part of the neighborhood effect. I'd want the partners to tell us whether it feels safe at all to ask about that through clinics, and what they need us to promise about who sees the data.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Marquez
transcript.text: Mm. One practical question for the city is whether we can keep enough location precision without creating a map that makes individual households legible. For analysis, I'd want to know whether a move changes someone's reachable canopy or park conditions, but we can- we could use protected addresses and only report aggregated exposure measures, if that fits what partners are comfortable with.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: Protected addresses and aggregate reporting are probably necessary, but they’re not the whole reassurance. People will want to know whether a clinic staff member, a landlord—obviously not a landlord—or the city can ever connect an answer about rent stress or depression back to them. We should bring a really concrete data-flow sketch to the partner conversation, rather than just asking them to sign off on confidentiality in the abstract.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Okafor
transcript.text: For the repeated survey, we should make the data flow clear before recruitment too, especially that clinic staff can help invite people but don't see depression, housing, or address responses. And if we use addresses for exposure, I'd want to separate those from the survey file as early as possible. Otherwise, people may reasonably hear "confidential" and imagine something much less specific.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: And the invitation itself needs to explain that separation in ordinary language, not bury it in consent-form prose. Marcus, before we decide on any optional biomarker piece, I'd want to know what residents would need to understand for that choice to feel genuinely voluntary, rather than feeling tied to getting care through the clinic...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Okafor
transcript.text: For a saliva-based stress measure, people would need to know it's completely separate from care and from the main survey, and that saying no doesn't change anything. They'd need to know what the sample can and can't tell us, and exactly who stores it and for how long. But if we do it at all, I'd treat it as a small opt-in pilot. The collection timing, privacy, storage, and compensation all have to be genuinely workable first.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Marquez
transcript.text: Mm, and for the environmental piece, I'd keep any address linkage completely separate from that optional saliva pilot too. We can probably calculate a protected, resident-level exposure measure—say, reachable canopy and park conditions—and then pass Marcus only the coded measures, not locations. But I'd want to check with the city how precise their planting and renovation dates and locations actually are before we—before promising that level of timing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: I’d rather not let the biomarker pilot dictate the whole study architecture. The core needs to work for people who reasonably say no to saliva, no to an address, or no to the housing module. And we should ask the partners whether those choices will actually feel separate in practice. Elena, the city’s dates matter a lot too. A ribbon-cutting isn’t the same as a park actually being usable, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Marquez
transcript.text: Exactly. We need at least three dates, when work begins, when the site is physically open or trees are planted, and when it’s actually, uh, usable. Plus, for trees, whether they’re still there at follow-up. I can ask the city if their project records distinguish those, because a planting completion date alone is a pretty weak marker of changed shade or canopy.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: Residents’ accounts of when it feels usable should count as a timing measure too, not just a city status field. A park can be technically open while people are still avoiding it because the lighting, rules, or policing changed. And the early interviews could give us a baseline on that before we call- before we call anything an intervention.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Marquez
transcript.text: I like treating that as a separate timing measure. The maps can show when the physical conditions changed, but not when the change became meaningful in daily life, so I'd line up our imagery and site checks with both where we can. I do need to check whether we can get comparable leaf-on imagery around those windows, though.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: And while you check that, I think the proposal can make clear that physical exposure is a bundle of measures, not just a single before-and-after canopy number. We should get the partners in soon, soon before we draft instruments, to ask what they need around governance, recruitment, and returning results, especially if residents tell us the renovated park feels less welcoming rather than more so.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Okafor
transcript.text: Mm. I think that gives us a defensible core. Baseline and follow-up surveys in all three neighborhoods, linked to protected measures of local change, with residents' use, safety, and housing context treated as part of the story, not noise. We should be careful in the proposal to say we're estimating associations over time, since even with the comparison neighborhood, moves and different follow-up- different follow-up rates can still shape what we see.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Marquez
transcript.text: Yeah, that feels important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Bennett
transcript.text: Good. I’d put one more thing in the core, not as an add-on. Brief baseline interviews and follow-ups with a subset of residents, so we can tell whether a change in a score means people are actually using the space differently or feeling pushed out of it. And before we lock down the methods too tightly, let’s get the partners’ terms for governance and return of findings. Otherwise we risk building a very polished study around questions they don’t want to...

realism_signals: interruptions, cut-off sentences, or people jumping in
imperfect coherence: tangents, small misunderstandings, points that get dropped or repeated
